entries.finding: A 2025 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis included 58 randomized controlled trials evaluating omega-3 supplementation and multiple adult cognitive domains.

Per 2,000 mg/day increment in omega-3 supplementation, pooled estimates favored attention (SMD 0.98; 95% CI 0.41 to 1.54; low-certainty GRADE) and perceptual speed (SMD 0.50; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.95; moderate-certainty GRADE).

The same dose-response meta-analysis reported improvements per 2,000 mg/day for primary memory (SMD 0.87; 95% CI 0.17 to 1.56; moderate certainty) and visuospatial function (SMD 0.86; 95% CI 0.46 to 1.27; moderate certainty).

Global cognitive ability improved in pooled dose-response analysis (SMD 1.08; 95% CI 0.73 to 1.44; low certainty), but the dose-response curve was non-linear, with gains increasing and then decreasing at higher doses.

The authors characterized the overall cognitive benefit as modest and noted low certainty for several domains; longer, well-designed randomized trials were recommended before treating the dose-response estimates as firm dosing guidance.

A 2026 systematic review included five randomized controlled trials reported in six articles (creatine n=126; placebo n=112), covering four trials in major depressive disorder and one in bipolar depression.
Creatine monohydrate was studied only as adjunctive treatment at 2 to 10 g/day for 4 to 8 weeks, so the evidence base does not establish standalone efficacy or long-term psychiatric use.
One major-depression trial found creatine plus escitalopram outperformed escitalopram plus placebo at eight weeks (Cohen's d=1.13), but this estimate comes from a single trial.

Creatine augmentation showed no difference versus placebo in one trial of female adolescents with major depression and no difference versus placebo augmentation in the included bipolar-depression trial.

Creatine was generally well tolerated, but two of 17 creatine-treated participants in relevant trials experienced hypomania or mania; the review called for larger double-blind trials across mental disorders.

A 2026 Cochrane review included 82 randomized studies with 10,613 participants; 72 studies involving 9,783 participants provided extractable data across cognitive complaints, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia.

In dementia, ginkgo versus placebo produced a small improvement on a short cognitive performance test at six months (MD -1.86; 95% CI -3.48 to -0.24), but heterogeneity was very high (I²=96%) and certainty was low.
In dementia, activities of daily living showed a small pooled benefit at six months (MD -0.19; 95% CI -0.35 to -0.03), with very high heterogeneity (I²=91%).
For mild cognitive impairment, the Cochrane review concluded that ginkgo probably has little or no effect at six months on global status, cognition, or activities of daily living.

In dementia trials, ginkgo probably produced little or no difference in overall adverse events up to 12 months (RR 0.95; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.00; moderate certainty) and may produce little or no difference in serious adverse events at six months (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.58 to 1.33; low certainty).
A 2026 systematic review identified 15 mood-disorder studies, with 10 contributing to meta-analysis; the evidence base included 14 randomized controlled trials and one open-label study.
The acetyl-L-carnitine review covered 809 participants (392 treatment and 417 comparator participants) across major depressive disorder and bipolar-disorder evidence.

Meta-analytic synthesis found acetyl-L-carnitine significantly reduced depressive symptoms versus placebo and reported efficacy comparable to standard antidepressants, while the underlying trials varied in design and population.

The review reported fewer adverse effects than standard antidepressants and subgroup signals favoring older adults and treatment-resistant depression, but emphasized the need for larger longitudinal studies before firm subgroup recommendations.
A scoping review of systematic reviews included 57 reviews comprising 227 meta-analyses of exogenous melatonin and human sleep-quality outcomes.

Primary-study overlap across the included melatonin reviews was low (corrected covered area 2.5%), indicating that the review literature drew from largely distinct evidence bases rather than repeatedly pooling the same trials.
Only 8.8% of included melatonin systematic reviews met all seven predefined methodological-rigor criteria, including protocol preregistration, dual screening, and bias assessment.
Among 215 meta-analyses comparing melatonin with an inactive comparator, 80.9% favored melatonin, 7.9% favored the comparator, and 11.2% had an unclear direction of effect.
Sleep quality was defined and measured heterogeneously across reviews, and few reviews evaluated overall sleep quality directly, limiting any single pooled interpretation of 'sleep quality' benefit.
Adverse events were commonly reported and generally mild, most often headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, and dizziness; inconsistent adverse-event terminology and reporting limited synthesis.
